_officialAuthorityConfirmation: The review's readiness record carries official_authority_refresh_required, and the refresh resolved the item the review itself called the top research priority in Ohio, in the opposite direction to the review's own finding. The review's first headline finding is that the internal reference's marijuana citation to ORC 2953.321 is wrong, because the official section of that number is "Divulging confidential investigatory work product". Section 2953.321 was read at Ohio Laws on 2026-08-06 and its official title is "Expungement of marijuana or hashish possession offenses", enacted by Senate Bill 56 of the 136th General Assembly with an effective date of March 20, 2026. The Legislative Service Commission analysis of Senate Bill 56, read at the Ohio Legislature the same day, describes the enactment of new section 2953.321 governing expungement of prior marijuana possession offences and places the filing fee at R.C. 2953.321(H), fifty dollars unless indigent, thirty dollars to the state treasury with half of that credited to the Attorney General Reimbursement Fund and twenty dollars to the county general revenue fund. So the internal reference's citation was correct, the review was reading the pre-Senate Bill 56 section of that number, and the substance the review had corroborated only in outline from the Moritz analysis is confirmed in the enacted section: the fifteen-gram hashish limit, the requirement that the conviction, plea or dismissal predate the effective date, the application contents, the forty-five to ninety day hearing, the prosecutor's right to object before the hearing date, and the fifty dollar fee. The marijuana track moves from "Additional research required" to implementable on that basis. One consequence for a listed-separately slot is recorded rather than resolved: the review's observation that section 2953.321 carried cross-references to ORC 2953.37 and ORC 2953.38 was made about the section that number used to carry, so it now points at a provision that has moved, while the status of 2953.37 and 2953.38 themselves is untouched and still unresolved. The review's second research priority did not close. A secondary source claims Senate Bill 288 created automatic sealing handled by the courts and the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation without petition or fee. It describes no automatic route. That is evidence against the secondary source but not proof of a negative, so the automatic-sealing track stays deferred and nothing is asserted in either direction. The review's structural findings that were confirmed by it are carried: "eligible offender" and the numeric cap on how many convictions may be sealed were removed by Senate Bill 288, so any product logic inherited from pre-2023 Ohio is wrong. tracks.legalName: Sealing or Expungement After a Not Guilty Finding, Dismissal, Grand Jury No Bill or Pardon (ORC 2953.33)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Ohio case that did not end in a conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: Where a person is found not guilty by a jury or a court, is named in a dismissed complaint, indictment or information, has a no bill entered by a grand jury, or receives a Governor's pardon, the person may apply to seal or expunge the official records. A not-guilty finding or a dismissal may be applied for at any time after the entry is made upon the minutes of the court or the journal, whichever occurs first; a no bill requires the expiration of two years after the foreperson or deputy foreperson reported it; a pardon may be applied for after the pardon or after its conditions are met. Each of these is expressly subject to ORC 2953.61. Relief is discretionary: the court determines whether a dismissal was with or without prejudice and, if without, whether the limitations period has expired, checks for pending criminal proceedings, considers prosecutor objections and weighs the applicant's interest against legitimate governmental needs. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.

exclusions: A dismissal without prejudice where the statute of limitations has not yet expired. That record is not ready and the participant must not be told it can be cleared.
Any incident where a companion charge from the same act has a different final disposition, until all related charges can be sealed or expunged together. ORC 2953.61.
Expungement, as opposed to sealing, to the extent division (C) of ORC 2953.33 limits it. That division was not read and is recorded as an open question.

controllingAuthority.summary: Ohio Revised Code section 2953.321, "Expungement of marijuana or hashish possession offenses", was enacted by Senate Bill 56 of the 136th General Assembly and took effect on March 20, 2026. The application identifies the applicant and the offence, includes evidence that the offence falls within the section, and requests expungement. The court holds the hearing not less than forty-five days and not more than ninety days after the application is filed; the prosecutor may object by filing an objection before the hearing date; and the court weighs the applicant's interest against legitimate governmental needs. Unless indigent, the applicant pays a fee of fifty dollars under ORC 2953.321(H). Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.

exclusions: Any conviction, plea or dismissal occurring on or after the section's March 20, 2026 effective date. The section reaches prior dispositions only.

Marijuana possession outside the specified divisions of ORC 2925.11.

tracks.legalName: Sealing of Conviction and Bail-Forfeiture Records (ORC 2953.32)

controllingAuthority.summary: A person convicted of an offence, or whose misdemeanour bail was forfeited, may apply to the sentencing court to seal the record once the waiting period for that conviction has run from final discharge. Final discharge means completion of the sentence, parole, all fines and all restitution, and "sentence" does not include payment of court costs, so unpaid court costs do not delay eligibility. Senate Bill 288 removed the definition of "eligible offender" from ORC 2953.31 and with it the numeric limit on how many convictions may be sealed, so Ohio is no longer a counting-caps state for sealing. Relief is discretionary: the court checks timing and pending cases, considers rehabilitation and prosecutor and victim objections, and weighs the applicant's interest against legitimate governmental needs. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
